summary: This bill creates a federal civil cause of action that lets individuals who received gender-affirming medical treatments (such as surgeries, hormones, or puberty blockers) as minors sue the providers for actual damages or $250,000 liquidated damages per instance plus attorney fees, when the treatment involved interstate commerce.

scores.thoughts: The bill creates a private civil right of action for damages but does not authorize, appropriate, or alter any federal spending. No connection to government expenditures.
No provisions address taxes, tax rates, deductions, or revenue collection.

The bill regulates access to specific medical procedures by imposing civil liability but does not engage with the public/universal coverage versus private/market-based healthcare dichotomy described in the topic.
No provisions relate to firearms, regulations, or gun rights.
No provisions address immigration, visas, borders, or protections for non-citizens.
No provisions address abortion access or restrictions.
No provisions address military or defense spending or policy.
No provisions address environmental regulations or climate policy.
No provisions address welfare programs, food assistance, or related benefits.
No provisions address schools, school choice, or federal education policy.
No provisions address drug decriminalization, legalization, or enforcement.
The bill establishes a civil cause of action rather than criminal penalties, sentencing reforms, or policing measures.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or globalization.
No provisions address deficits, debt reduction, or fiscal policy.

The bill creates civil liability for providers of gender-affirming medical treatments performed on minors and defines such treatments in detail to restrict them. This directly limits legal access to and protections for gender-related healthcare for transgender youth, pushing strongly toward the +1 end of the spectrum.
No provisions address foreign aid or international assistance.
No provisions address voting access, election integrity, or electoral procedures.
No provisions address technology regulation, data privacy, or digital oversight.
No provisions address worker protections, union rights, or employer flexibility.
The bill does not reference religious exemptions, civil rights enforcement, or conflicts between religious liberty and anti-discrimination rules.
